audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both Dotton & Wagner sentences are verbatim in the PDF we hold, sec. 2.5, printed pp. 14-15 (PDF pp. 20-21); the McCollum & Chen p. 291 sentence is verbatim in the now-downloaded open-access JIPA PDF. (2) The deciding source is a 2018 75-pp grammar sketch, but the classification (fixed final, in the dominant set for morpho-lexical exceptions) matches every description opened today: Özçelik 2015 (instrumental, multiple Kazakh speakers: final prominence, duration-cued, right-edge iamb), Özçelik's Brill encyclopedia entry ('accent in Kazakh falls on the final syllable of a prosodic word'), and McCollum & Chen 2021's literature summary (Balakaev 1962:78; Muhamedowa 2015:285-288 = final). Two caveats worth a caution line rather than a reclassify: (a) Özçelik reports weight-attracted non-final stress in some roots 'in some varieties' (kép.ka, ʃe.gírt.ke) and analyses Kazakh as weight-sensitive iambic — fi

sources.quote: p. 291: 'Descriptions of Kazakh have typically suggested that stress falls word-finally in the language (Balakayev 1962: 78; Muhamedowa 2015: 285–288). Kirchner (1998: 320), however, argues that Kazakh words bear two accents, a word-initial stress accent ... and a word-final pitch accent ... others contend that Kazakh does not have word-level stress, but rather only phrase-level prominence (Dzhunisbekov 1980, 1987; Abuov 1994: 41–42; Vajda 1994: 644–647).' sources.citation: Özçelik, Öner. 2015. 'Stress' or 'intonational prominence'? Word accent in Kazakh and Uyghur. Turkic Languages 19(2): 163-192. doi:10.13173/TL/2015/2/163 (author-posted copy, oozcelik.pages.iu.edu).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Regular prominence is word-final and moves right with suffixation (almá, alma-lár, alma-lar-ím, alma-lar-ɨm-dá:); production experiment with Kazakh speakers finds final syllables significantly longer (duration the correlate, not intensity/pitch), analysed as a single weight-sensitive iamb at the right edge ([LL(LH́)]). Adds: 'at least in some varieties of Kazakh, syllable weight is crucial ... heavy syllables attract stress' (kép.ka, ʃe.gírt.ke, der.ba.zá:, sa.rɨm.sák), and pre-stressing suffixes (negation -MA, question -MA, copula/agreement) give exceptional non-final stress.

sources.quote: 'As with most Turkic languages, accent in Kazakh falls on the final syllable of a prosodic word. As such, each time a suffix is added to a word, accent appears to move to the right' (almá ... alma-lar-ím-dá). Notes accented syllables bear greater duration, apparent root exceptions align with syllable weight, and pre-stressing suffixes (negation, question particle, adverbial -ʃA, copula/person agreement).
